utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. On Friday you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I remind you today once again that you are still bound by that declaration. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Today we will continue with your examination-in-chief. The protective measures as assigned by the Trial Chamber are still valid. I appeal to you not to directly refer to the function you had. If need be, we may turn into private session. There is another thing I have to ask you, and that is that both of us should take care to pause between question and answer in order for the interpretation service to be able to catch up with what we are saying. Thank you. On Friday in response to my question, you talked about how the electoral rallies affected the behaviour of the population, how it changed the population in the area of your service. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described the way in which the population started -- treated you differently; you, the person who had worked there for a long time. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These electoral rallies, did they in any way effect a change in the conduct of the population vis-a-vis the other members of the population in Drnis and with regard to the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events that took place in relation to electoral rallies caused the population to fear -- caused fear in the population, not only on the part of the members of the police station but imagine how great the fear must have been on the part of the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there reason for them to start feeling differently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. I would equate it to a plague, because the fear did not appear out of the blue. It gradually grew. It was caused by Serbophobia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you cite an example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can cite several examples. The last time I mentioned that there were different nationalist songs. All these types of conducts were sanctioned by the Criminal Code; however, the instructions the police received were not to react to such types of behaviour because in early 1990s, still the instruction was to prevent any firing up of nationalist sentiments. There were songs to the effect that Serbs should be hung from a tree. For instance, we received a postcard card featuring a nationalist -- a national park of Krk. There was this picture featuring one area and I can still the -- Klucica [phoen] and still to this day you can see that picture. I want to say another thing. Up until 1990, the police reacted most strongly in reaction to nationalist excesses regardless of who the perpetrators were. These nationalist insignia that were sanctioned were mostly the swastika, the Ustasha sign "U," and the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The reports arriving to the police station on such types of behaviour, did their numbers increase?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, there were two sources of such behaviour. First of all, the Serbs would come to the police station to ask as to what the state would be doing to prevent such behaviour. There were also anonymous reports but these were mostly from the Croat population and these reports were of a provocative character. Those were the two types of reports that came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said the latter reports were anonymous and provocative. In what way do you mean that? I believe this is quite relevant for the case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you an example of that. In addition to Catholic churches, there was one Orthodox Church in Drnis, and on that day there was some sort of an Orthodox festivity - I don't know which one - and traditionally, church bells chime on that day. We had about 200 or even more anonymous reports to the effect that public law and order was being disrupted and -- to the effect that such types of conduct would no longer be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You did not explain to us in what way it was thought that the public law and order was disrupted and what caused you not to react to such reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, customs and religious ceremonies do not constitute a disruption of public law and order. If that were the case, then even the sound of a passing car would constitute the disruption of law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would not wish to be myself to be the one to infer conclusions but rather I leave it up to you. So what was it specifically that the citizens were complaining about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This category of citizens did not mind the chiming of the bells but rather the Serbs who were honouring their religious observance. It was, in short, the Serb population that they had problems with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will leave it at that but let me say this, that they minded the fact that the bells chiming were the ones on the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That was what I said. It was the Orthodox church that was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did this event take place? I'm referring to -- or actually I have in mind the part of the year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific but it may have been April or May, sometime in that part of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you had been working for the Drnis police station since 1975, and this was 1991 -- 1990. Had there been any such reports before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, because on the occasion of such Orthodox religious ceremonies, you didn't find only the Serb population in front of the Orthodox church but also the Croat population and the community in general. This had been the case up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to complete this topic and to avoid any misunderstanding, you said that Drnis had mixed Croat and Serb population. Does this mean that there were Catholic and Orthodox churches in Drnis? Is this what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Drnis, there used to be one Orthodox church, as far as I remember, and two or three Catholic churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And up until 1990, the relations were harmonious; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I apologise for the interjection but this is one of many leading questions so far and I think counsel could get the same answers just by asking things in a non-leading -- non-leading way: "How were relations?", instead of, "Relations were harmonious, weren't they?" It's just example of many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received very direct answers by this witness to that effect. I merely wanted to wind up the topic because the witness was discussing these matters very specifically in answer to questions that were not leading. My point of departure was that whatever the witness thought was quite clear, might not in fact be as clear to us and that was why I insisted on the question and this sort of situation was not ordinary. In my understanding it was quite extraordinary, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you're talking about, Mr. Milovancevic, but I've said to you before, if you want to refer to a statement the witness has made previously you've got to say so. You've got to link it up to that statement, not just come up with a statement out of the blue which suggests that you are leading the witness. You know? You've got to link that statement; if it's a repetition you've got to link it to a previous statement. But as for what you are saying, I just don't understand what you're saying. I'm not quite sure you're addressing the objection. In the circumstances, I will therefore uphold the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I will proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were the interethnic relations like in the everyday life, in the street, in cafes, and so on and so forth? Did there come a time when there was a change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there were significant changes. People no longer went to have coffees together and so on and so forth. In the -- in Drnis there were a dozen cafes, perhaps, but only two of them were frequented by Serb citizens because otherwise they were exposed to provocations. One of these cafes was owned by a Croat and the other one by a Serb. Eventually this cafe owned by the Croat experienced a lot of difficulties, especially because of the fact that Serbs used to drop by. In public transportation, in stores, at workplaces, the situation was the same. There was this separation process along ethnic lines because people no longer trusted one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything that changed in the human resources policies of the police station in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't the case only at the police station, in the municipal government, at -- in the judiciary, you would have a change in terms of the fact that the Serbs were dismissed and Croats took their place. In the police station, the same thing happened because the chief of the station was replaced by a Croat who did not have as many years of experience or as many skills as the incumbent person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately in what period of time did this take place, the reference point to be the elections in May 1990. When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station, the change took place in February. That's to say before the elections. As for the other institutions, these replacements took place before, during and after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you're mentioning these replacements, can you tell us, if you know, what was the reason for the dismissal of the persons who had up to that point been holding these positions and the arrival of new ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main precondition for the replacement of these persons was the ethnic and party affiliation of the people. Primarily the political affiliation. If the person was a member of the HDZ, then he would be appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about this happening in Drnis but did this also happen in other parts of Croatia, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, based on what I heard from my friends, this process took place throughout Croatia. Even later on - I believe it was in April or May - for instance, at the police high school, the management there was replaced by some new personnel. I even heard cases of these hitherto professors who had been thrown out of their offices and their residence in Zagreb without being allowed to take their belongings. As far as I know the people who replaced them came -- were actually outsiders. They came from outside of the profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these were outsiders. Do you mean that they came from abroad or do you mean that they simply came from a different environment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I primarily had in mind the countries abroad, like Germany, Australia, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The people who arrived from abroad, which ethnic community did they belong to? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission I'd like to explain this in detail. They were part of the Croatian ethnic community, and were mostly emigrants; not economic emigrants but political emigrants. Some of them had been involved in sabotage activities before the multi-party elections and were active from their centres in the United States or wherever they were. They were committed to the Ustasha ideology and for the most part were members of terrorist organisations and were classified as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were classified as terrorists. Where did you get that information from? Does it come from your service or did you come by that information in any other way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, you're asking a leading question, Mr. Milovancevic. You started very nicely, where did you get that information from? That's where you must stop. The remainder of that sentence, then, is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I accept your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will rephrase my question. Where did you get the information from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, see, I did not go to Zagreb at that time, and I did not see this firsthand but the police officers who used to work in Zagreb and left Zagreb, they had personal contacts with these people and they were the source of the information I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these persons were members of terrorist organisations and you also used the term Ustasha. Do you know how long such organisations had been in existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, extremist Ustasha organisations had been in existence ever since the year 1945, when the Ustasha army fled the area, leaving for different parts of the world, Munich, Canberra, Perth, and other parts of the world. There they created terrorist organisations and there are many examples of sabotage terrorist actions carried out in Yugoslavia, ever since 1945. The last such action was, I believe, in 1988 in Drnis, in my hometown, and this was a sabotage action that was directed against a monument erected in the memory of a national hero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Vladimir Rolovic ring a bell in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vladimir Rolovic belonged to HOS, I believe. I'm not sure. This is therefore an extremist Ustasha nationalist organisation, and I believe he assassinated a Yugoslav ambassador, Mr. Trolovic [phoen]. Or, rather, I may have been mistaken in the ambassador's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because in your answer you said that both the assassin and the victim were named Rolovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I may have been wrong there, about the ambassador. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: An operation on the Radusa mountain, does that ring any bells? Of course, if you cannot recall it just give us a very brief answer; let us not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually studied such operations at our courses and in our instructions -- instruction manuals. We read a lot about it and I have talked to some colleagues who participated in that operation, which actually was the arrest and the conducting of other actions in relation to a group of some 19, I believe, terrorists, whose task was to carry out sabotage operations in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. They were supposed to assemble at the Vran mountain in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina and then proceed on from there. That sabotage group was liquidated, I believe, except for the youngest participant who was arrested and was put on trial and convicted and sentenced to some years - I don't remember how many - but one of those members of those groups organised an attack on JNA tanks in the area of Kupres, and that is about my knowledge of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is not important but could we have dates for these episodes? Otherwise it's since 1945 is all we know at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is an incontrovertible fact that we are talking about 1945 and the period thereafter, when we talk about the terrorist activities of the Ustasha emigres and their coming to Yugoslavia. I just wanted to see whether the witness had any specific knowledge about that topic, generally speaking. I have no specific questions apart from this last situation described by the witness. I should just like to learn from him who these terrorists were. I'm just trying to verify a fact that these were indeed members of a terrorist organisation who came, as he said, in 1990 to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you then contextualising in terms of time, these events around 1990? Is that where we are supposed to concentrate, 1990? From 1945 to the present moment is a very long time, Mr. Milovancevic. You've got to give us some time when you're -- that you're speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is correct. I am referring to 1990 and that is my last question also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the operation on Radusa mountain which you talked about a while ago, do you recall the exact period of time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whom did you have in mind when you said that members of the Croatian emigre circles were coming, arriving in the country in 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, to the -- to my knowledge, it was precisely from those circles, from those extremist emigre circles, that they sent people, i.e. from which people came. It was actually such criminal circles, as it were, that actually financed the HDZ for a good part. I should also like to say that there were sabotage actions also in 1968 when two policemen were killed on Mount Velebit apart from this one in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Drnis as the city in which you served. Can you tell us whether there were any military facilities, any military installations of the JNA, that is, in that town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite near, perhaps some three kilometres off Drnis, there was a naval barracks and below it was another depot. I don't know how many soldiers there were. That was some two kilometres farther away than that. So it was in the vicinity, in the immediate vicinity of Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You -- when you mentioned this storehouse, this depot, to whom did it belong? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The naval barracks belonged to the naval military district. They held some ammunition and resources necessary for the navy, whereas the depot belonged to the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the relations between the police station, your police station, and the JNA like until 1990, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our relations, according to our rules and the -- generally speaking, were more than correct and that was so not only with the army but also with all other structures, with the judiciary, with other public services. With the social work centre we had exceptionally good and correct relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the period in which you discharged your service in Drnis, from 1975 to 1990, what are your impressions about the attitude of the Yugoslav People's Army which maintained and held those facilities and the local population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1990, the relations between the members of the Yugoslav People's Army and the members of the local populace were excellent. Many officers from all over the former Yugoslavia were on duty there, many of them got married there and stayed on in Drnis and there were no problems whatsoever between them and the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the relation in terms of the competences or the jurisdictions of the police and the army? Was the one in control of the other or vice versa? Can you tell us something about that particular relationship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was regulated under the law. Military security organs, as they were called, they regulated issues within their own facilities, within their own compounds, and this was under their competence. Public security organs on the other hand, which is to say the police, were in charge of, of course, public law and order, traffic control in the broader territory, and such issues. But if you will allow me, this relationship was actually disturbed as of 1990. But, of course, I'm jumping ahead of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So these relations as you say were regulated by laws and regulations. Were they harmonious until 1990? Can you describe them as harmonious?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely harmonious, absolutely by the book, by the law, and according to all the custom which governed this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in 1990 in relation to that particular relationship? Were there any changes at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, in the army itself, among the officers themselves and between the citizens and the officers, between the population and the officers, there was so -- there arose mistrust. I have a specific example. Actually I didn't realise immediately at the time what that was about but in 1990, I believe it was in April, the state security service of Croatia, of the Republic of Croatia, undertook some security assessments -- security assessment, of course, is an operation to regulate and assess the defence of specific facilities in a specific moment of time in relation to sabotage and such other groups. So in April there were two operatives of the State Security Service of the Republic of Croatia -- yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please slow down, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were two operatives of the State Security Service who came there from Sibenik, and they undertook this security assessment of the barracks in the place called Trbovnija [phoen] quite near Drnis. As these were people unfamiliar enough with the terrain, they approached me to assist them in their task. I did help them, but I found it quite strange when they told me that for their particular -- that they -- that the military security organs should not know that they were there and doing that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When they told you this, did you ask them why that was so or did you just -- did what they asked you to do for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask them anything. We just had such relationship of cooperation that we didn't doubt one another, did not suspect one another. I did find it strange but I did understand why that had been so in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that you understood why that had been so only in 1990? What particular circumstance led you to understanding that situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in August and September in 1991, precisely that barracks was attacked by the forces of the HDZ, the National Guards Corps, meaning that they had actually been collecting data, gathering intelligence, for the attack on the barracks which was to ensue by paramilitary forces a year after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just another question: You say that state security was collected [as interpreted]. State security belonging to whom? When they were controlling this security situation around the barracks, as you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in organisational terms, the security -- the state security does not belong to any MUP. It does belong to the MUP of Croatia but it is a specific department, a separate department. So they operate from the centres, from Split, Karlovac and Osijek, and also subcentres or departments like Sibenik and some smaller places so they did not belong to the MUP, they directly belong under the republican SUP, the Secretariat of the Interior, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was your position when the HDZ won the elections in Drnis municipality and came to power? Were there any changes in terms of your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were provocations, you see. I will give you a concrete example. My superior from the SUP of Sibenik didn't bother me, he didn't make any changes. He did offer me certain positions which I could not accept. However, in the field, itself, there were quite a few provocations. So I would go to tour the traffic patrols and, for instance, I would go to a cafe for a coffee, midnight or any time after that, 2.00 in the morning, and there would be -- there was a company of Croats sitting at a table and people that I was on good terms with prior to the war. One of them told me, "You still dare come to this place?" And the other ones actually tried to calm him down, "Oh, come on, don't pick up on this guy." So you can see how secure I was. I was carrying arms, and I was in that kind of a situation. So what could the other Serbs, other Serbs who did not wear arms, expect and how secure would they feel to be going around?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber wants to remind you that according to your estimate of this witness's time, it's three hours. You're approaching almost half of that and it's about time we switched over to the Prosecution to cross-examine. I'm going to have you keep you on toe this time, after that experience of the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have promised to reassess the time that we need for this witness and for witnesses. This is one of exceptionally -- of the exceptionally important witnesses. So by your leave, I would like to proceed. I have a number of very important questions which I should like to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As long you finish during this session so that the Prosecution can cross-examine after this. Got to keep to that three-hour estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the situation -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter didn't hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know anything about -- and then the interpreter didn't hear you for the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The question was: Does the witness know anything about the armaments of the reserve police force at the time we are discussing which is 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know something about that. I know what the situation was like and I'm going to explain it for your benefit. I don't recall what month it was exactly, 1990, the MUP of the Republic of Croatia adopted a decision that from all municipalities with a majority of -- majority Serbian population, the armaments of the reserve forces should be seized. That meant Dalmatia, the municipality of Obrovac, the municipality of Benkovac, the municipality of Knin. They did not touch my municipality because the majority population was Croatian. In Lika, Gracac, Korenica, Lapac, in Kordun, Vojnic, Vrginmost, the municipalities, and other municipalities up there on the Banija, Dvor Na Uni, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- were these arms, were these weapons, taken, seized? How did this situation resolve itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were seized in places. I'm not sure what particular municipalities. That was quite a long time ago. But at any rate, the reaction of the Serbian population of the Serbian police, was vehement because this was an illogical decision. I believe that they took, seized the weapons in Obrovac and other municipalities, I'm not quite sure which ones at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the reaction of the Serbian population or is it the reaction of the Serbian police or is it the reaction of both?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this attempt at seizing the arms of the reserve forces led to a reaction. Can you describe whose reaction it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was the reaction of the Serbian population because the Serbian population was desperate because a truly new Ustasha state was nascent, with all the elements that that entailed, so this weapons of the reserve force was their last hope that they would be protected in a way by some sort of a police from an imminent future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the police towards this action of seizure of arms of the reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police also shared the position of the people. The police also would not accept this to happen because the police, of course, was in the service of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the erection of roadblocks in 1990, barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know. I'm aware of that having happened. I was on duty that day. There was some sort of a gathering in Drnis, as a matter of fact, and we could hear the special Croatian police units were heading towards Knin to seize the arms of the reserve police force there. The people were increasingly in fear from day to day and there was an unorganised erection of roadblocks on roads in Drnis municipality. For instance, in the place called Klanac. If I remember correctly, there was a truck which they placed across the road and some sort of logs also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation -- in connection with this obstacle near Drnis, this roadblock near Drnis, do you know what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That obstacle that barrier was between Drnis and Knin municipalities, in a place of Klanac, between Kosovska Dolina and Petrovo Polje. This is where this block, roadblock, was erected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Drnis police station take any steps with regard to that particular barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the barricade was erected on the 17th of August 1990 by a group of younger men who were controlling the situation there, to inform the population in case the special police forces were to make an incursion into the area. This was on the boundary between the Knin and Drnis municipalities so the police did not take any steps until the 20th of August. Therefore, three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you therefore tell us what it was that happened three days later on the 20th of August 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of August 1990, the Sibenik SUP secretary, Ante Bujas, and the chief in Vugosic [phoen] came to the Drnis police station with a special unit, some 30 strong. The reserve force of the police had been called up. I only did the night shift that week and it was at 7.30 in the evening that I came to work that day, and I saw the reserve force equipped with weapons and live ammunition. As I entered the office that belonged to the secretary there, I found between seven and 10 inspectors there who were partly members of my station and partly members of the Sibenik station. Ante Bujas chaired the meeting. There was a police guard at the door, who I didn't know, and I was no longer able to leave the room once I entered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, was Ante Bujas, your superior, the superior of all of you, was he issuing you with any orders at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to say that. As soon as I came, Ante Bujas said, "Gentlemen we have been given the order to neutralise the barricades in the Klanac area. The JNA, the Presidency of the SFRY, are in session and have decided that the barricades be proclaimed illegal. Milan Babic" -- and I don't know if he mentioned Milan Martic was arrested and some officers of the JNA had been arrested. "We must head for the barricades to destroy them and, I repeat, you are permitted to use any and all means available to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how did you understand this order that all and any means were available to you and you were free to use them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the order was quite clear. We were free to proceed to kill the persons manning the barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation developed in a way I will never forget as long as I live. It was a very difficult situation. I told Bujas that if this should indeed be the case, that I would myself take an official vehicle to the barricade and I will personally arrest these young men and bring them to the station. I told it him that we should not use any force and that this should be solved with political means. Bujas's answer was quite strong, and he said, "No and no and no. We have to settle this once and for all." If you'll allow me I would like to tell you the whole story about the barricades and how it all happened. It's a very simple story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bujas therefore set out a plan. I was supposed to take a group of 40, 50 or 60 police officers and approach the barricades from the south-western side and hit the right flank of these people. I don't think there were many of them and they only had hunting rifles, nothing more. My colleague had -- who had to say -- have the same number of men was supposed to approach them on the right-hand side and then a group of special police officers were supposed to use a drey [phoen], and they were supposed to throw teargas at the men, at the men manning the barricades, and I also heard that helicopters were supposed to land later on to the north of the barricade and kill all the people. Of course, later on we found out that there were some civilians there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did this particular meeting at the police station end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to intervene and suggest that the action take a different course. However, Bujas insisted that I take along all the police officers, there may have been even 70 of them, including the reserve force. He proceeded to inform all the police officers of the plan and repeated the plan in the same way as I had heard it. The people's reaction was a negative one. They hooted and said that they did not wish to kill their own people. I have to say that the police officers were members of Croat population, Serb population, even some Muslims. All of them started laying down their arms saying that they would not go against their own people. One of the Sibenik force even brought a rifle into the room but there was one of our inspectors who took the rifle away from him. Another police officer was carrying a machine-gun and he was walking to and fro outside at the door. We practically chased the special police unit and their superiors out of the area, out of Sibenik -- out of Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the order issued by Ante Bujas carried out or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was not carried out and this was thanks to the intervention of the members of both the active and the reserve force of the Drnis police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did the Yugoslav press report on the event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the Yugoslav press covered this particular event in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself give a statement for the press to tell them precisely what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief in my answer. That night, my house was fired upon, and these were really the most difficult days of my life. If I had to ever -- if ever I had to go through that nightmare again I would commit suicide. I read in the papers that some police officers recounted these events the way I told them now; however, Ante Bujas denied these stories. And I felt compelled to call a press conference and, in 45 minutes, I retold these events to the journalists in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The information conveyed to you by Ante Bujas that it was the SFRY Presidency and the JNA's decision that this action should be carried out and these people killed, did you double-check whether this was indeed their decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We doubted the information given by Ante Bujas and we actually, based on the intelligence we collected, realised that the truth was quite different. There were a couple of police officers who were in my police station and who were tasked with assassinating me and some others. Their idea was that all of us together should attack the barricades and in the process they should kill us. So that the HDZ-led armed forces should finish us off and that, the following morning, they would all inform the general public of Yugoslavia and say that it was a gang of people who attacked the Yugoslav police. So that was the purpose of the action, this misinformation and to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have an article from a newspaper that was published on the 28th of August 1990. Could we have the usher's assistance in distributing these articles to the Trial Chamber? And they talk about the -- the article talks about these events. We have copies for our learned friends from the OTP and for the Trial Chamber. Do you have before you a text published in Politika Ekspres, the date is the 28th, and it says Knin? It bears signatures of some persons. Can you tell us what this text is about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, this is a letter to the journalists recounting the events of the night. Over 25 police officers confirmed that the information contained there was true, with their signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this be tendered as a Defence exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 899.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I wanted to ask you one thing. I believe we started 20 minutes late today. I believe that I should be given these 15 minutes, that I am entitled to them, and that I should perhaps use them after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did we start 20 minutes late or did we start ten minutes late?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 minutes, in fact, I believe, Your Honour. I believe it was around half past 3.00 and we can double check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You've got --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what the reaction of the Drnis population to this -- these events was or the reaction of the population in Krajina, in general, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly after these events, a -- certain Croat citizens came to me to congratulate me on thwarting this action; however, there were different situations as well. Several days later, 2.000 people gathered in front of the Drnis police station and criticised the Drnis police for not carrying out their duties properly. I will tell you another story. I had one member of the reserve force whose wife was a Croat. There were quite a few mixed marriages in where I lived. He had one child. The moment his wife heard that he had refused to go and kill Serbs, she abandoned him and never spoke to him again. That was how strong the hatred was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Had the town of Zadar ever belonged to the territory of Krajina or the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the period between 1990 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, never, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a town that had mixed population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the town of Zadar does have a mixed population, with a very significant size of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is the same true of the police station? That's to say the Zadar SUP. Or was the situation the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the same period, a similar situation arose in the town of Zadar which resulted in the police officers of Serb ethnicity fleeing the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My question to you was whether the workforce in the Zadar police station was also of mixed --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe this was true for all the police stations. There was never a one-population workforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at the Zadar police station letter? This is number 0280-8282, an OTP document that we had translated. We have for 142 signatures by people of various ethnicities, members of the MUP Zadar, who sent an open letter to the president of the Republic of Croatia, to the Prime Minister of Croatia, to the Minister of the Interior of Croatia, to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, to the federal executive council and the federal Interior Ministry of Yugoslavia. All of this transpired on the 5th of November 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The number is 0280-5282, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be distributed to the OTP and the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the document before you, Witness? Do you have before you the open letter by the Zadar police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HDZ was in power at the time in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the HDZ was in power in Zadar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This letter was sent to all these addresses in Yugoslavia and I will read out to you the first three paragraphs and I will have a question in relation to that. The first three paragraphs in the English language can be found on page 1. "Why is the weapons from the Zadar police depot taken out and distributed clandestinely at night to Croat civilians in the municipalities of Zadar, Obrovac, and Benkovac? Why, after the MUP Croatia order to activate the reserve force" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that they don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "the reserve force of the police. Why are the weapons and ammunition distributed to the persons that had not been previously designated for that purpose?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the interpreters just indicated that they don't have a text from where to read. You would have to go very slowly for them to interpret. I don't know whether you intend to read all that because now you've given it up. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. Only three paragraphs and one after that. I think we have an extra copy that we could give to the interpreters, if that can be of assistance to them. We should have one copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would certainly be of assistance to the interpreters, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, they're happy to take one of my copies. At this point, though, I would object that there has been no foundation laid for how the witness knows anything about this letter which is from Zadar. He hasn't testified that he was from Zadar, he didn't work in Zadar. It's not clear he knows anything about what's happening. He just said that he'd heard of something like this, but at this point I would object to lack of foundation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, lack of foundation alleged for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness testified about the admission of new members into the reserve force of the police and their arming. I was interested in this phenomenon in general. I'd like to know whether the witness has any other knowledge about this matter dating from that time so I'm inquiring about the general situation and about the witness's knowledge about it. The witness also talked about the situation in the police station in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have not told anything about the foundation you're laying for this document, Mr. Milovancevic. This whole explanation that you give has nothing to do with the question of foundation. The closest you do come, and you're still miles away, is when you say the witness also talked about the situation in the police station in Zadar. That doesn't lay a foundation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could also respond briefly, as far as I can see on page 25 there were three questions asked about Zadar, and the witness prefaced every answer with, as far as I know. And to me that indicates that, well that there hasn't been a foundation laid for how he could have some useful information to share with -- about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic [Microphone not activated]. ; this might be a convenient time to take the break. Maybe you can think about it during the break and decide what to do with this document when we come back. Thank you very much. Court adjourned, come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, have you thought what you want to do with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I withdraw my question and I withdraw the document. Thank you. This is what I intend to do at this particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to ask you a question, at the outset, by your leave. I have assessed the time I require for the gentleman who is at the stand here in the capacity of witness. Can I ask the Trial Chamber to grant us an additional half hour in addition to the time already allotted to us in order for me to properly finish my interrogation. If that would be all right with you, I would be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got 15 minutes. You have 15 minutes, Mr. Milovancevic, I'm afraid. Sorry. Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, our position on this would be it would be nice to have a procedure set up. Gather that Defence counsel is going to provide a revised list of estimates of time and in the future perhaps we could work on that. We would not be opposed to a request for additional time as long this was justified with an explanation of why is more time was necessary, precisely, or the best estimate of how much time is necessary and things like that. And I spoke to Defence counsel about this, and we wouldn't be opposed to them making such a request under those circumstances. I just wanted to put that on the record because I had spoken with Defence counsel about it, although I think if such an application is made, it would be appropriate to excuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the thing. And because I don't want to excuse the witness now, you've got to say to me now whether you -- do you have any strong objection to me -- to Mr. Milovancevic having an extra 30 minutes? And we can sort out the question of times later. The reason I'm going the way I am is precisely because we need to look again at the 65 ter list of the Defence, in view of the changes that have occurred and most probably give a revised 73 ter decision. And right now, because of that fluid situation, that's why I'm going on the original estimate, estimated time, by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a one-time thing, I would not be opposed to an additional 30 minutes, understanding that this has not been -- that this will be dealt with in a systematic way in the future. But for this particular time I'm not opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have 30 minutes, Mr. Milovancevic, 25 to 5.00, I stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you referred to a situation related to an order for an armed attack on a roadblock near Drnis. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened then in the public security station in Drnis after that? Can you tell us briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this order was refused in the police station in Drnis, we had the Sibenik forces abandon the station and flee in the direction of Sibenik, and the members of the public security station of Drnis took over control. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bujas, as the chief of the Sibenik SUP, when he was transmitted to you -- transmitting to you this order of attacking with arms the barricades, did he tell you whose decision it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bujas told us, and I repeat, that the Presidency was in session, the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in session, and it had outlawed the roadblocks and issued an order. The president of the Supreme Command; that is, the Presidency as the Supreme Command to the units of the JNA and to the police units to dismantle the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Milovancevic, I'd like to find out -- my apologies. I'd like to find out from Mr. Witness, the gentlemen - Nenad, is it? - who you said came to the station in his bathing trunks and had had a breakdown and told you those things, was he in the throes of the breakdown when he said those things or had he had the breakdown before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, well, this is a sort of a caricature on my part. When I say that he had suffered a nervous breakdown, what actually was at work were his pangs of conscience. He had come to apologise to his colleagues, and he actually was supposed to kill us and that is why he came. He came to say that that was -- actually, what he wanted to portray by his behaviour was how monstrous an order it had been and that he was supposed to carry out such a monstrous order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So when you said that he came there in his swimming trunks and had a breakdown, you weren't intending to convey to us that he had a nervous or mental breakdown, then? This is a breakdown of morality? Or it's a breakdown of conscience, rather? Because I just want to understand fully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I couldn't say that he had actually suffered a nervous breakdown. I'm no doctor and cannot say that with certainty, but it is a question of conscience because this was a man of high morality, Mr. Metesi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just pick up on what you said. You have made the declaration to tell us the truth and nothing else but the truth. Please refrain from using caricatures in characterising your evidence. Tell us honestly what you know, what happened, without giving any caricatures. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the mention of the mentioned Metesi, did you ever refer to him in your earlier statement in connection with the situation when the order was issued for the barricade to be attacked with arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention Mr. Metesi because in the yard of the public security station of Drnis, he was walking around in that yard with a machine-gun in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When he came later, as you say, in his bathing suit, what was he saying in connection with his role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw Mr. Metesi with a light machine-gun, we didn't know what his task was. However, he didn't go with us into the meeting room where we were having a meeting and were being issued orders. He only came after an hour. And then he told me and explained what his task had been, and it had been to kill those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, it is being suggested that maybe page 31, line 6 to 7 needs to be edited. I'm not quite sure. Can we just have a look at it and say whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. Yes. I fully understand. It crossed my mind a while ago. Yes, I'm sure that needs to be done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May then page 31 line 6 to 7 please be edited out? Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to present to Your Honours, to the Trial Chamber, and to my learned colleague the Prosecutor, this decision assigning the witness to a new work post, but -- and after handing you a copy, a hard copy, because we do not have an electronic version, I should like us to move to private session for a bit because of the text of the decision itself and the possibility of the witness being identified on its basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Again, I'm being asked to ask you to direct your attention to page 31, lines 13 and 15. Just look at them and tell me whether you think they require redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe of course that it would be certainly recommendable for it to be redacted. Thank you. I failed to react at the right moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it. Then lines 13 to 15 of page 31, may they also be deleted? Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you see in front of you a decision brought by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. It bears a date and the number. We do not have to read it out although we are in private session. Does this decision refer to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this decision refers to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't seem to have asked that we move into private session. Are we in private session? We are not in private session. May the Chamber please move into private session. I'm sorry, about that, Mr. Milovancevic, I was still looking at other things.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before you is a document with a date in the top corner, 14th of October 1990. It is an audio recording, it says, and this is a section of a conversation between ministers Martin Spegelj and Josip Boljkovac. So this is a text in relation to which I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. Martin Spegelj says, "Listen, if the need arises, say, in a crucial moment, find two or three men to get rid of the most dangerous ones." Josip Boljkovac says, "Okay.". And then Martin Spegelj goes on to say, "To get rid of them physically. Somebody goes to the flat, a courier. He appears at the door, bang, bang, bang, and goes down the stairs." To this Josip Boljkovac says, "And then they can call the police and ask them who did it." To this, Martin Spegelj replies, "Then down the stairs, goes to another one and then kills him. That is at the same time. The most dangerous ones can be killed at the door step. Never mind about women and children. None of that." Was this the film that you say you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the film I saw. I saw it twice, as a matter of fact, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let me say this again. If that's the point you wanted to establish, that's not how you do it. You ask him first to tell you what it is he knows. That's why we keep on saying, lay the foundation. By the time you show him this document, he must have told you what he knows about that film and if he's able to quote these things then he can quote them before he looks at them. For you to show him this and then say is this the film that you saw, it's leading. I wish you could respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I remember correctly, the response -- the previous response of the witness, he said that he had listened to the conversation of these two officials, that he has -- had seen the film. It is a fact that I didn't ask him about the details of that conversation. There you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the detail you must ask about and confirm that in fact what he says he knows is what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any other details which have to do with this conversation and this film? Was Knin mentioned in it? Do you recall that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. It's been a long time. I recall some details. I might not be as precise as necessary, but they said something to the effect of Knin will be easy to crush. We'll crush Knin, something along those lines, but I can't be precise. It's been 16 years since. Or Knin will be the last one we'll deal with or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The details you mentioned also stemming from the conversation of these two persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the conversation between Spegelj and Boljkovac, as far as I can recall, but don't hold me to that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at page 13 of the document in the English version. On page 13 of 22 of the English translation, Mr. Josip Boljkovac, Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia says the following, according to this transcript: "We are going to use all means. We are going to use weapons and the Serbs in Croatia will never be what they have been so far. Their supremacy is history. Their Knin is not going to be Knin any more. We will take over Knin. Knin is going to disappear." The sentence goes on as follows: "All the Croats should keep this in mind. We will establish a state, no matter what the price is going to be, and no matter if blood is spilled." This is one portion of the text. And another portion of the text which is uttered by Minister Spegelj on the 14th of October 1990, and this is page 14, "This is the way we will solve the issue of Knin. We will massacre them and we will receive international recognition for it. We will butcher them. Especially now that the son of a bitch in Serbia" - and he's referring to Milosevic there, and so on and so forth. Do you recall these details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recall the film that was broadcast and I recall the discussions among people who were very much frightened by the film and what it contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these people arrested and were they brought to trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they never stood trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the illegal imports of arms, the illegal trafficking in arms, in that period in Yugoslavia, 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that it was in the month of October 1990 that a contingent of arms arrived in Croatia. Part of it was distributed to HDZ activists in the area of Drnis. Part of the weapons were transported by members of the civilian protection of the municipality of Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the exercise, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the purpose of the exercise was for Croatia to build up its own armed force. The same situation existed in 1945 as it did in 1990, and that was to create an armed force to resist the Serb population in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the month of September, you moved to Knin from Drnis after all these events. What was the reaction of the population to all of these events in general, or of your family in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of August 1990, my family fled the area because on the 26th of July 1990, my house came under fire. I was really on my guard throughout the time because I was afraid that my family was going to get killed, that I was going to get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. You said that your family and you yourself came under fire. Who was it who fired shots at you? You worked for the Drnis police station. You had an employment there. Who was it who opened fire on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of July 1990, I believe it was, it was after midnight, past midnight, a car went past my house with two persons in it who opened fire at me. It was later on that I found that the chief of my police station fired at me and hat -- what was later to become -- who was later become the assistant Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know their names and how did you establish their identities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the shooting incident, I reported this event, and some police officers conducted the investigation to the effect that they were supposed to obtain witnesses who would say that no gunfire was heard on the night, so as to come to a conclusion that I had falsely reported this. Smiljan Reljic was the person who became later on the assistant of the Minister of the Interior and my chief was Zoran Perica. Later on, the investigation did not come to any results although there was reasonable suspicion to doubt that the two of them had been the perpetrators of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it that this ended like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was a peaceful person at the time. And I wasn't the only person who came under fire. There was a Croat aged 70 who had also come under fire because he came into conflict with Perica for his peaceful views and I believe he came into conflict with him in 1990 and I believe that they fired shots at my house because I followed my own consistent views and did not wish to abide by what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that your family fled the house. Where was it that you resided in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I resided in the Tepljuh neighbourhood. I served in the police at the time and when I came back home on the 17th of August, my family was no longer there. They fled to my brother's who resided in a village two kilometres away. It was because in that recent period that we felt uneasy because my dog barked throughout the night, we had the feeling that someone was around the house, and I relocated my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you moved to Knin, did the accused in this case, Milan Martic, work in that public security station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found myself in a very difficult situation. I had no where to stay. I didn't know where to go. My brother could not take me in because my wife was already there and I -- he had two small children, and I applied to Mr. Martic and some other colleagues I knew from before to help me with accommodation. They offered me some cottages but, however, in the meantime, a relative of my wife's came up with an apartment that he was able to give me to stay in while I was in Knin. So I stayed with my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more questions, Your Honour, by your leave, to finish the examination of this witness. I am nearing the very end of his examination but I would like to finish one theme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: For how long were you on the police force and did you come to know Mr. Milan Martic? What kind of a person is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Martic and I were born in the same year, 1954. I had known him for 30 years. I have known him for 30 years. And his reputation was a very good one. At the time, he was considered a person of very broad-minded views and of moral integrity. I believe that Mr. Martic was like myself, of left-wing positions and his station was mostly manned by persons who were not extremists but rather of a moderate centre-left views.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Martic exhibited any sort of intolerance towards anyone, especially in terms of interethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, at the time, there was no place for persons who discriminated against people in our station. I know that in 1989, during the 600th anniversary of the Kosovo battle, he exhibited intolerance for any sort of discrimination, even if it was exhibited by the Serb population. In this way, he was against any discrimination whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. It has been suggested that maybe lines 3 to 15 at page 34 should be redacted. Can you just have a look at that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is vague enough and it is not sufficient for the witness to be identified. If you're of a different opinion, I am not opposed to redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I have no opinion actually. I just wanted your guidance. Maybe for safety's sake, shall we redact those lines, then? That's page 34, lines 3 to 15. Thank you very much. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Mr. Black, I'm one of the prosecutors on this case. I'm going to be asking you some questions. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, you just talked a little bit about the accused Milan Martic. I was wondering, when was the first time you said those things to the Defence counsel? When did you first give them your views on Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was when we discussed Milan Martic, when we met for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was, approximately? I don't need an exact date but just approximately when it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a month or a month and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also testified not too long ago about an incident where someone actually shot at your house. Do you remember when the first time was that you discussed that with the Defence counsel? Or with the Defence investigators, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a month or a month and a half ago, in Belgrade, because I didn't know Mr. Milovancevic before that. I talked about my case when I met him, simply because I didn't know the man before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that. Another detail that you mentioned about this person Nenad who actually came back, the Croat who came back after the episode on the 20th of August 1990, was that another thing that you discussed with Defence counsel when you met with them before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One correction, though. I don't know whether Nenad Metesi is a Croat. I really don't know what his ethnicity is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise. That was an assumption on my part. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to complain as I did on one past occasion, that many of these things that have been testified today about today do not appear on the 65 ter summary. Things that do appear on the 65 ter summary have not been covered, and maybe that's because there wasn't enough time for counsel to get everything, but I specifically asked Defence counsel for a supplementary information sheet, and they did give me one. It provided a little more information, but these are details which obviously were known to the Defence, were not provided, and it's consequently almost impossible for me to cross-examine on them. I'm not asking for a delay. I'm going to go on with the other cross-examination that I provided, and hopefully on the breaks I can make up for that. But I just would like to say that a procedure was established and we hope that in the future it's complied with, providing this supplemental information to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the information we submitted to the OTP could certainly have been more detailed, but it was produced under the time constraints and in the conditions in which we were. We tried to cover all the topics and for some other events we considered them to be matters of common knowledge. We gave a certain range of topics and events and we considered them to be sufficient to put the OTP on notice about the testimony. It was not our intention to hide anything from the counsel by not furnishing them with the details. It was merely that we were under great pressure to honour the time limits. The initial summaries we gave were even more general and we simply tried to respond the best way we could under the circumstances of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I just want to warn the Defence that, you know, proceedings at the Tribunal here, like in any other court or Tribunal, are carried out in terms of certain procedures. And the procedures prescribing how we run proceedings in this Tribunal are contained in the Statute and the Rules of this Tribunal. Now, we cannot run this proceedings -- these proceedings efficiently if at every turn you're going to be telling us that you were not able to do A, B, and C, because of the terms that you're working under and you expect at every turn the Chamber to accommodate your failure to comply with Rules of Procedure. You knew -- there are -- you have a team that works with you. I see no reason for you at times to be all three in court, if I may say so now. I've held myself from saying so all the time. When some of them are not doing anything in court, when they could be in the office doing these very things that you say you don't have time to do. And if you come and sit all in court, the assumption is that you've done your job. Now, you -- here is -- we are now in a situation where the Prosecution is saying to you that you didn't mention these things in your 65 ter and yet you have the time to lead them in evidence. How are they supposed to cross-examine on them? To think that things are common knowledge is neither here nor there. Common knowledge, if it's common knowledge, why do you lead it in evidence at all? It's common knowledge. But if you're going to call somebody to testify on it, then you've got to mention it in your 65 ter summary that I am going to call -- lead this witness on this issue. Common knowledge or no common knowledge. It is no reason to leave out information that you intend to lead in court. It is no reason that you are working under certain pressure to -- not to be prepared properly. We all worker pressure. We all have to meet deadlines here. You're not the only ones.
