Now, I hope this is the last time I hear about this because I think the Chamber will have to look at very drastic measures to get your team to fall in line, if this continues. Sorry, Mr. Black, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, what do you want to say, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We provided the information we considered to be normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have told me that and we don't have time. We've got to finish quickly. I don't want you to repeat what you've just told me. You told me what information you provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is one other matter I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't repeat what you told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the working schedule of the Defence team is distributed between the members of the team. Now, it is quite rude and incorrect to say that something was not done simply because one of the members of our team is absent. We have divided our work and are trying to do our best to perform our duties properly and not to place our learned friends in a position where they are surprised by some topics that they were not put on notice about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is being rude by saying that something was not done simply because one of the members of your team is absent?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Mr. Milovancevic stated -- said "strong" or "harsh" rather than "rude."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presented my view that the assessment about someone's presence or absence and about this being used as the basis for inferences about someone's work cannot simply be made because one cannot know and have a full insight into the work load carried out by each and every member of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may be so. That's not the only basis and I've given you many bases as we've gone along with this case, Mr. Milovancevic. You know. And I don't want to say much about this with the witness here. Maybe if you want to take this up we can do it after this witness is finished. I would like this witness to be cross-examined and done with. Can we please go ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me go on with some questions for you now. You testified that in 1990, the HDZ held some political rallies in connection with the elections, where fascist songs were sung and Ustasha salutes were seen. You remember testifying about that, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the latter part of your question? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course. In 1990 -- or you testified that in 1990 the HDZ held political rallies and that at those rallies, fascist songs were sung, you could see people giving the Ustasha salute, and other things like that, right? You remember that now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then you also testified that most Croats, they refused to use that kind of language or those kind of symbols and they even denounced it, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say most Croats. I said some Croats left that rally. This was the rally at Grac, and they said this is really ugly. We don't want to be here. And I observed this. It wasn't most of the Croats. It was some of the Croats. But at the time, you wouldn't even be able to say most of the Croats acted this way because this was just several thousand Croats who were present at this rally and this was just the early days of such rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Even beyond this rally, there were a lot of Croats who didn't accept this kind of language, they didn't use it and they didn't support it, right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I can't talk about this in figures. I can tell you that a large part of Croats did accept this. Now, whether this was 60, 70 or 80 per cent of the Croats, I can't tell you. I wasn't in a position to know this. Of course among the Croats there were honourable and honest people who were bothered by such statements but let's say there was a gathering of 3.000 Croats. You can't say that all of the Croats were there, that 99 per cent of the people were behaving this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, and that was also true about the HDZ, wasn't it? There were extreme elements and then there were other, more moderate elements, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there were moderate elements in the HDZ but there was just a handful of them, you know. I saw people who condemned such a conduct and who said they didn't want to be in such a nationalist party as HDZ was but these were just a handful of them. I recall that the president of the municipality wept and was very sorry about what had happened to me when they -- when there was this incident and so on. But -- or there was this other person who took my cap, my police cap off, and said no more stars here we are going to have chequerboards, and so on and so forth. But this was the one person, the one isolated incident. Not all the Croats were like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I understand you. Are you saying that all Croats except for just a handful, just a very few, were fascists or are you agreeing with me that there were actually quite a number of Croats who weren't fascists who didn't support that kind of idea nor those kind of symbols? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never believed that all Croats were fascists. There are good and bad people in the Croatian as in any other people but there was this euphoria that had spread among the masses of the Croatian people fueled by the propaganda which was the order of the day, and carried by all the mass media and also propagated at various meetings and rallies. There was fascists much course, among the people but the Croatian people is a good people, as a people. I've never met a bad people, speaking about peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you one or two questions about media because you mentioned it. In fact the Serb media focused on those most extreme elements at these Croat rallies, isn't that right? That was the part that they really focused and paid attention on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian media as well is, like the Slobodna Dalmacija, the Free Dalmatia, wrote quite correctly, quite realistically about the situation, and the paper Danas also wrote about the situation quite realistically but the situation in the field was much more complex, much worse, than portrayed by the media, believe you me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just try to have you focus on my questions. It's important that you listen closely to my questions, okay? What about Serb media? They focused on those extreme Croat elements, didn't they? That was one of the main focuses of their reporting, rather than on the moderate Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many Serb papers, and I read the papers of both, not too many because of my work and the constraints with time, there were articles which were out of the -- of a certain line. There were individual cases like that, which focused more on some aspects of the situation, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can get a clear answer to my question because I'm not sure that you've answered it. You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that at least parts of the Serb media focused attention on those extreme Croat elements? Do you agree with that or do you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot fully agree with you, Mr. Prosecutor because no Serbian paper actually tried to pinpoint the extremist elements on the Croatian side, but there were individual articles that could -- that were out of this regular, so to speak, line. Not -- neither the Tribjun Novos [phoen] Theme, nor Danas, nor the dailies actually focused on these extremist phenomena on the Croatian side, but there were individual instances of such articles having been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about leaders, and especially Serb leaders in the Krajina. You would accept that the Serb political leadership focused on that extremism among the Croats as a way to kind of motivate the Serbian population to vote for them, right? You would accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I do not accept that at all because this does not correspond to the truth in my view, because when we talk about the arming of the Croatian paramilitaries and if I talk about what was actually the beginning of a civil war in Yugoslavia, if I talk about the extremist excesses of a resurgent fascism, of course the other side cannot look favourably upon all that. In my view, the Croatian side had a purpose, had an objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. I wasn't asking you about the Croatian side. I was asking you about the Serb side and I want you to try to focus on my questions, okay? That will help us go through this more quickly. Do you deny that the Serb political leaders played on the extreme elements of the Croats for their own political gain to try to generate Serb nationalist feelings? Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I do partly deny that because the Serbian people in Croatia, during the multi-party elections, voted overwhelmingly for a pro-Yugoslav or pro-Communist Party rather than a Serbian party, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which party was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the SDP, the Party of Democratic Change of Racan. It was a Croatian party, it was not called a Croatian party but it was a party which deceived the Serbs because by placing their confidence in that party, the Serbs were simply betrayed. They actually lost what they had hoped to get. There was another party, Mile Dakic's party and there were some other parties that they voted for. I'm not quite sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact Serb politicians who were elected to office in those parties then abandoned those parties, didn't they, and they joined the SDS? That all happened in 1990, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Serbian politicians, the Serb politicians, when they came to the Sabor to the Croatian assembly, they were humiliated and sent out, driven away, so they left the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1990 or late in 1990, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you about one other thing that you said. You suggested earlier that all the Croatian -- the Croatian people, the Croats that returned from abroad, that those were mostly fascists. Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, that all the Croats who returned from abroad were fascists. I said that there was a part of members of extremist emigre organisations who came back and created chaos. But I never said that all of them were fascists and nor would I ever, nor will I ever say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me just read you what you said at pages 8 and 9 of the transcript, and maybe I just got the wrong impression and you can correct it. You said, and this is in reference to people coming back from abroad, you said, "They were part of the Croatian ethnic community and were mostly emigrants, not economic emigrants but political emigrants. Some of them had been involved in sabotage activities before the multi-party elections and were active from their centres in the United States or wherever they were. They were committed to the Ustasha ideology and for the most part were members of terrorist organisations or were classified as such." Now, if you want to change that testimony, please go ahead and clarify it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about specific target group, not about the Croatian people or Croatian emigrants in general. I was talking about a specific group which was connected with extremist core groups throughout the world. I was not talking about the Croatian people. The Croat people in general, I never want to say anything bad about that people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another thing you said in your testimony earlier, you said, and I'll quote you, "A truly new Ustasha state was nascent." That's the way you felt then and that's the way you feel now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they -- if these groups were calling themselves Ustasha, if they celebrated the letter U and the chequerboard, if they saluted using the fascist sign, how else should I call them but by the name which they call themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you see, my confusion -- well, are you suggesting that all Croats were calling themselves Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat, not all the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because you keep making generalisations, like you talk about an Ustasha state and then you say they were calling themselves Ustashas but not everyone in the Republic of Croatia was an Ustasha or called themselves Ustashas. That can't be what you're saying, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert, I repeat, I cannot call the whole people -- I cannot call any people a negative name. But the formations which were illegally coming into existence in the 1990s in Croatia which illegally armed themselves, who wore these insignia and emblems were Ustashas in my book because they called themselves Ustashas, because they were Ustashas indeed, and they are Ustashas to me today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another thing that you said in your testimony was that you basically said that -- well, a couple of times you equated the Ustasha government of 1945 with the Croatian government of 1990.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my modest historical knowledge, and I was born to an anti-fascist family, we never forgot the massacres suffered at the hands of the Ustashas because in 1945, they -- in 1941, they massacred a very good part of the Serbian people. So it is upon the same principles or perhaps upon similar principles that the HDZ was coming into existence and actually held its public events and had public manifestations with the same trappings as the 1941 Pavelic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With all due respect to the suffering of Serb and other people in the Second World War, what you're saying now in this focus of Serb leaders on equating the Croatian government with an Ustasha fascist government from World War II, the constant references to genocide and Ustasha, that was -- that was a political manoeuvre to create fear in the Serb population, wasn't it? It was a common Serb propaganda technique in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Distinguished Mr. Prosecutor, a while ago, ten minutes ago, the Defence counsel was actually reading out what the -- Spegelj as the Minister of Defence and Boljkovac as the Ministry of the Interior, namely members of the Croatian government, what kind of an agreement they had, which was slit their throats, kill and there will be no Serbs. Why -- what else should I say? Why shouldn't I equate them? What is the difference between Spegelj and Boljkovac and these people from 1941, Brdak [phoen] namely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Since you made reference --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Budak, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- what Spegelj and Boljkovac were actually talking about, they were actually talking about an operation against JNA, they weren't talking about killing Serbs or Serb civilians, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, they actually used different names, when they were talking about the killing, they considered the Yugoslav army the Yugo-Chetnik or the Serbo-Chetnik armada, they actually were referring to Serbs. Because in 1991, a number of the officers of the Yugoslav army of Croat and Slovene ethnicity left that army although it was an army based on parity, namely based on the number of inhabitants. In 1991, in my assessment, the Yugoslav army had perhaps a majority of Serbs because they had left, so this was something which did not suit Spegelj. It was no longer his army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you saying that these things that happened in 1991 were Spegelj's reasons for saying something in October of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sorry if I misspoke or if I spoke in haste. So in April 1990, my colleagues whom I know talked -- came to me and we cooperated very well, and they had carried out a security check. Had they talked to the organs of military security, that wouldn't have been suspicious to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you but you already testified about that so it's not necessary for us to repeat that testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I think that much is clear. That was by way of preparations for what was to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one more question on this and then I think I'll move to a new topic but just to clarify: You're not saying that extreme comments or the use of extreme symbols by the HDZ or other Croats could have justified crimes committed by Serb police or armed forces, right? You're not saying that that would justify crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I condemn every Serb crime, every crime by an individual, whether a soldier, a policeman, or a civilian, and, to my knowledge, and I spent all the time there in the area, I heard that there had been crimes. But there were no crimes that were instigated by the state or by the legitimate authorities. But there were crimes, and I would be the happiest of men if all of those crimes or rather the perpetrators were to face this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were no crimes by police or by armed forces against -- Serb police or Serb armed forces against Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that. That's not what I said. There were individuals in whatever uniform. There were individual crimes. But it wasn't a state that was the instigator or the principal, the orderer of these crimes for Croats or any other ethnicity, people of any other ethnicity to be killed. That was a civil war and it was a terrible situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So just so I'm clear, I guess you're saying that any time that a Serb policeman or a member of the Serb armed forces committed at crime against Croats or against anyone else for that matter, then they were just acting individually, even though they were wearing their uniform? Is that what I'm supposed to understand from this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that any commander had -- or any chief of police had issued any orders to the effect that harm should be inflicted on anyone else. But in the units of both parties, there were criminals, there were murderers, there were bad people, and as I tell you I would be happy to have all those people face justice here and to tell them who was it that ordered them to kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just we are going to take a break in a second but one question. You would agree with me that those people should have been brought to justice at the time, not just here at The Hague but they should have been -- if people commit the crimes in 1990, 1991 and up to 1995, they should have been brought to justice, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For criminal offences of that type, it is never too late but they can be brought to justice only when the conditions for that exist. I believe that many people of those who did -- who committed such crimes have already been sanctioned but of course we should never let the matter rest until all have been brought to justice irrespective of what side is concerned, whether it is the Serb or the Muslim or the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We will take a short break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, the last couple of questions I asked you started with a question and I don't think you answered it so I just want to go back to it, and the question was essentially this: Whatever you say that the HDZ did or said, that does not -- would not justify crimes by Serb police or Serb armed forces, is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in my assessment, this is partly true. The HDZ created such an at sphere whereby it caused a civil war, because I am deeply convinced that the war in Croatia was a civil one. I believe that the HDZ pursued such policies as committed a crime against peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you're saying that these policies that you say constituted a crime against peace, that that justified crimes, war crimes or crimes against humanity by Serb police or Serb armed forces? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I condemn any crime regardless of who perpetrated it and I still assert that. A crime is a crime regardless of who it is committed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I understood that. You said you condemned all crimes. I just want it to be clear for my own understanding whatever you said that the SDZ -- HDZ did it would not justify those crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree that nothing can justify crimes, murder, regardless of who it is perpetrated by, if someone's life is taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And even crimes less -- you know, where someone's life is not taken but other crimes, you would agree that those aren't justified under those circumstances, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I fully agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we, I think, leave this topic of the HDZ and you talked about the -- what you called the extreme elements and you recognise there were some more moderate elements but it's true, isn't it, that the HDZ was mainly focused on independence for Croatia? That was their primary goal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was their primary goal and I would add, through illegal or unlawful means or extreme means. This was no democracy. This was a rule of force and violence. [Realtime transcript continued with answer in error].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you're aware that in the public documents, and public statements of the HDZ, they consistently included protection for the rights of all citizens, right? Regardless of ethnicity? You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was fictional. This was a lie that was presented in the public whereas the situation in the field was quite the opposite. If you have the HDZ creating armed detachments, if over ten years in my police station we had issued ten licences for weapons and if with the rise of the HDZ we were issuing as many as 20 weapon permits a day, exclusively to the members of the HDZ --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And am I to understand that in your view, if there is arming of the population and things like that, then whatever the political party says on its face you need to look at what was really happening to judge the party or its motives? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conduct exhibited by the leaders of this party characterised by an anti-Serb view, and the arming of extremists, which was adding fuel to fire, then you can make only one inference from that, which is that the Serbs had to be exterminated in Croatia, just as in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if you just changed one word there, and you said that there were leaders of a party characterised by anti-Croat view instead of anti-Serb view, there was arming extremists and adding fuel to the fire, then there would be only one inference that, right? That that party had nationalistic goals as well? And the party, as you can guess I'm referring to, is the SDS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I can't equate the HDZ with DSS. That would not be logical. The DSS was being created in the conditions of necessity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're aware also - one last question about the HDZ - that the HDZ, one of their positions is that they were seeking international recognition for Croatia, for an independent Croatia, right? They were sort of courting the international community for recognition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you go on to another area, Mr. Black, just intervene to make a correction. At page 61, line 7 to 10, a question posed by you was subsumed as part of the answer to the witness's previous question -- to your previous question, the witness's answer to your previous question. So that should be corrected at page 61, line 7 to 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's in line 7 where I say -- it was actually me that says, Well, you're aware that and then it continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope that's clear for the record now, and I believe it can be corrected in the review of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn your attention to August of 1990. You -- actually could we go into private session just for briefly, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our language, you would use a different term than the one I used for my wife's brother.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, just a quick reminder. We've been in private session so we were very free to talk about, you know, your relatives and things like that. Now we're back in open session so just be aware of that, please. You testified that there were barricades erected in Drnis or around Drnis on the 17th of August 1990. Did you personally participate in manning those barricades or in organising those barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't among the organisers of the barricades. However, in view of the fact that these were people who were my neighbours, I went past these barricades several times and everyone could have. It was -- the purpose of these barricades was simply not to -- to prevent a possible attack from the Croatian police, whereas commercial traffic, any other traffic, was able to pass there. I heard stories about it although I had nothing to do with the barricades, I didn't participate in the manning of the barricades or in organising them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever try to pass by a barricade with a Croat in your car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, believe me when I say that I do not remember but it is quite possible that I did because Croats went there and Muslims, everyone. As far as I recall, the control at the barricades was directed solely at the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you never heard anything about Croat civilians having difficulties at the barricades, being harassed, having their cars searched, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories that some Croat civilians had problems that they experienced by some individuals manning the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of problems did they have, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they amounted to the searches conducted in -- of the vehicles but I did not hear of any brutal conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Other than the barricades near Drnis, did you -- I guess you didn't ever see any other barricades in other parts of the Krajina, is that right? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not move about much. The barricades were not erected only at this one spot I was referring to. There were barricades along the boundaries of practically all the municipalities. You could even go as far as to give this overstatement that even children were erecting barricades. This is of course on the part of the Serbs but later on the Croat side started erecting barricades just as the Serb side did in some villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me focus just on the Serb barricades and really I'm focused on August and September, maybe up even to December of 1990. Police also participated in manning these barricades, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police patrols, as far as I remember and recall, were not supposed to be at the barricades all the time but to encourage the persons manning the barricades to behave in a civil way because every day there was the increased threat of Croats attempting to take control of these municipalities, and the idea was that this should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when you say that police patrols were not supposed to be at the barricades all the time, am I right to understand you that police were at the barricades some of the time, uniformed police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't give you a precise answer. I believe the situation was just as I described it now but I couldn't -- I can't remember that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Milan Martic had assumed command of the barricades on or after the 17th of August 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment and to my knowledge, I never heard that Martic had assumed control there because the barricades were not Martic's or anyone else's for that matter. The barricades were organised by the people. These were the villages along these particular roads, but I had never heard of Martic having assumed control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about a defence -- or a staff for the defence of Knin which was later renamed the Council for National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what the name of the staff was but I did hear that there existed a body which, I don't know, took care that the Croatian forces should not break through and get into the area but I don't know what it was called really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was Milan Martic the leader of this staff that you've -- that you kind of recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that either because I don't know the title of the staff, its members, or its whereabouts. That's why I can't tell you whether Martic was a member of the staff or what he did for that matter, because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me give you just a couple more details to see if it jogs your memory. If it doesn't, please just say so. The staff for the defence of Knin which was later called the Council of National Resistance was set up on the 17th of August 1990 and its tasks included sort of coordinating the barricades, they operated from Golubic and some other places, and it was headed by Milan Martic. Does that ring a well? Do you remember hearing about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I might have heard about it but so much time has passed I do not remember these details because after all I spent most of 1990 being medically treated. In fact, that treatment continued into 1991 and I had my own problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I understand. Is it fair to say, then, that there could have been things happening in Knin and in the Krajina at that time of which you're simply not aware, you just don't know about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One specific thing: Were you aware that on the 17th of August 1990, Milan Martic and others handed out weapons at Golubic? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as weapons and Knin are concerned, the only thing I heard was that the Knin SUP did not surrender the arms to the members of the army of the Republic of Croatia but that they took it themselves. But what happened with it afterwards, to whom they gave it, I really don't know. But I did hear that the police or the citizens took the arms, took the weapons, from the police station. I really don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember it was the police, right, it was the Knin police, that had taken those weapons, is that -- is that what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I wasn't there. I really don't know. I know that the weapons were taken out of the station. It was no longer there. When I returned to the station, and re-assumed my duties. But I cannot say whether it was the police or the people. I think it was the people, that the people barged into the police station one evening and seized the arms. The police would not open fire at the people. The people went into the station, seized the arms in fear of a possible attack, and I believe that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Because the way you originally stated it was the only thing I heard was that the Knin SUP did not surrender the arms to the members of the army of the Republic of Croatia but that they took it themselves. Is that what you remember? Or are you now saying you remember it differently? Or you don't remember at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the army of the Republic of Croatia did not exist at that time at all. In 1990 there was no such army at all. You are asking me to remember. I heard but I did not see for myself any of those things because I had only learned by hearing of that, that the people had gone into the station and seized the arms. I didn't see that for myself with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're quite right about the army of the Republic of Croatia. I was reading from the transcript so I just note that perhaps at transcript 72, line 17, there may be a mistake but we can look at that. I think it's clear now from what you've stated. You heard, in fact, didn't you, that it was the police that had organised the seizing of the weapons from the Knin public security station; is that right? That you actually heard that it was the police that did that and made it look like the citizens had broke in? Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That doesn't sound right. That is not what I said. I said that I wasn't aware, that I didn't know whether it had been the police, but what I had heard, what I had heard subsequently, is that the people had gone into the police station and seized the arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say you weren't aware and you didn't know whether it had been the police. Why, then -- what made you think that it could have been the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, there were some policemen there at the time, at least the people -- the policemen who were on duty that night. Of course, they could not oppose these people, put up a resistance to these people, because I heard that that night there were thousands of people who had gone into different police stations throughout Croatia with the same purpose in mind, to seize the arms from those -- those police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let's just focus on Knin. I think when you talk about thousands of people in different police stations, unless you have something specific in mind, please don't speculate. Don't exaggerate. Just talk about what you know and let's focus on Knin. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand you but you are asking me questions about a period or rather about events that I myself did not attend. So everything that I'm telling you is from stories that I heard, and there were all kinds of stories being bandied about so I have no material proof to corroborate anything that I'm saying because as I said I didn't see any of those things with my own eyes. On the 17th of August I was still in Drnis at my workplace and also on the 18th and on the 19th and 20th of August as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your response. Let me ask you about some things that happened after the 17th, 18th, 19th, and 20th of August. Did you ever become aware that the Knin police station knew that Serbs were illegally arming themselves but they weren't willing to take any steps to stop that illegal arming? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, during that time, during the four days that you refer to, I was, to put it that way, virtually a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you actually because I -- I just interrupt you because I think there was a misunderstanding. I was actually asking you about after that time, so after the 20th of August, after that middle part of August, did you hear about this afterwards, between -- let's say up until December of 1990, that the police station actually became aware of Serbs illegally arming themselves but they weren't willing to take any steps to stop that? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see some civilians wearing arms, automatic rifles and semi-automatic rifles, I could see such civilians around. Whether this was the result of police action, I don't know. I'm quite sure that it wasn't because there were about 50 policemen in the Knin police station, and as for people who were fearing a possible Croatian aggression or a Croatian crime were about 30 to 50.000. So that that kind of a police force with those numbers couldn't certainly have opposed that many people because what happened in Knin was the people happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one question for clarification. You said you saw -- you could see civilians wearing arms. You're referring to Serb civilians, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to Serb civilians who were manning the barricades, as I mentioned I passed by the barricades twice or perhaps it was more than that. I cannot remember. But -- and they were bearing arms. Now, whether those were weapons from the station or not, I cannot say that. But they were bearing automatic rifles and of course no ordinary civilian in the former Yugoslavia had such manner of weapon at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said earlier you saw civilians wearing arms, automatic rifles, and semi-automatic rifles. Did you see civilians at these barricades with that kind of weaponry? I know you've said you've seen them at the barricades with automatic rifles but did you also see them with semi-automatic rifles and wearing arms, whatever wearing arms means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the barricades, at first, they just had hunting rifles and later they had automatic rifles and semi-automatic rifles which the men manning the barricades wore, and I'm -- I believe that those were seized from the police station. It is plausible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, sticking with this issue of arms, did you ever hear the figures that 1300 guns and 400 pistols had been infiltrated into Knin and Obrovac municipalities after -- sometime after mid-August 1990? Just did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually I can tell you a name in that connection. I have heard. I heard about it. Is this a closed session? Can I mention some names and is it -- can I at all ask for us to move into closed session, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At the witness's request, may the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified about how you actually went to the media and publicised what had happened in the Drnis police station, right? You talked about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a press conference where I made a public statement for the duration of 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that was -- that was actually against police regulations, wasn't it, to make an unauthorised public statement like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under ordinary circumstances, this would have been unlawful. I would have been reprimanded or punished in a way, but these were not normal times. This was quite something different. The attempt was to prevent people from getting killed. This was an attempt at averting a conflict and a war, and this was the most -- the grandest such attempt because it was carried out by Serbs, Croats and Muslims alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in fact, as you say, you weren't reprimanded, you were actually -- you requested to be transferred to Knin and that request was granted. That's what happened afterwards, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, after that, I was suspended which means I was not reassigned to Knin; however, several days later, probably after some political factors had a second thought about it, they reassigned me to a post in Knin which was by two or three notches lower to the one I had before and they said that this was done at my request and I assure you that no man who is in his right mind wishes to run away from his home because after death, this is the worst fate that can befall you, to be expelled from one's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So what it says in the document that we looked at earlier about you requesting to be transferred to Knin, that's false, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was true, because I was cornered, because I had no other option but to ask to be reassigned from Drnis. But I wasn't the only one who was reassigned. All the other police officers who took part in this so-called mutiny, both Croat and Serb police officers, were reassigned to Zagreb or Slavonski Brod or other places some 15 days later. But they no longer worked at the Drnis police station. There remained only others who were of some other ilk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did that seem somehow unfair to you that you would be -- you would suffer some consequence of what you just called a mutiny? You weren't dismissed from your work, you were simply transferred somewhere else, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was transferred to the Knin SUP, but my actions of the time are the object of my pride even today. On the 4th of January 1991, together with all my colleagues, I don't know how many of us there were, all of us were dismissed. So all of us who were transferred to Knin were dismissed on the 4th of January 1991. I lost my job then and I had already lost my home, my house, without ever having committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, on that same day, the Knin SUP was created separate from the Croatian Ministry of Interior, right? And Milan Martic was appointed the secretary for the Interior of the SAO Krajina. That's why the policemen in Knin were, as you say, dismissed, because they had established their own rebel police station, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is your opinion. My opinion is that this was no rebel station. We didn't call ourselves police, policija, we called ourselves, militia, milicija, which means in Latin "armed people" or "people's army." And we wanted to be the people's army because up until then, we were municipal police. We served the citizens of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you didn't expect to remain in the Croatian MUP when the SAO Krajina had declared that the Croatian Ministry of the Interior would have to -- no longer have jurisdiction on the territory of the SAO Krajina after the 5th of January, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a matter of the point of view. This was something that should not have happened, because this could have worked still, but the Croatian MUP got rid of the Serb personnel because the police officers from Dubrovnik were not in Knin, the police who worked in Zagreb were not in Knin but nevertheless they were dismissed. People aged 36, all of them were retired and they were retired simply because they were unsuitable for the Croatian police and they were not standing accused or they were not guilty of any barricades or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, isn't it the case that by August of 1990, Serb police in the Krajina, in Drnis and in other parts, were openly defying the orders of the Croatian MUP? They were basically deciding which orders they felt like implementing and which they did not? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that perhaps you might have been wrong in the year there. I think you said 1990. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I meant, that by August of 1990, based on what we've talked about, on the 20th of August 1990, as well as what happened in Knin and in other places, Serb policemen in the Krajina were openly -- openly disobeying orders from the Croatian MUP and deciding for themselves which orders they wanted to implement and which orders they didn't, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-116 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, no. I told you that in my police station, there were Serbs, Croats and Muslims. Therefore, it wasn't just Serbs who refused to carry out orders that were not consistent with moral values because orders to kill people are not moral. Had the Croatian MUP been entitled to issue such orders then I would draw a parallel with the German regime and its policy to kill Jews. Just as they were not entitled to kill Jews, so Croats were not entitled to kill Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic, you've got two minutes to 7.00. I don't know if you want to begin with your re-examination or whether you want to skip it over to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are at the very end and if I would have questions, then they would only be several. I don't know if the Trial Chamber would have questions for the witness. I suggest that we resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. Then we'll resume tomorrow. The Court will be adjourned and we will reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in this court. Am I right? Yes. It had been indicated earlier that we will start at 10.00. We will start at 9.00 tomorrow. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
